# Question 1

Below, I simulate a rather quite annoying set of regression data.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(0510)
n <- 250
dat.q1 <- tibble(x1 = rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10),
                 x2 = factor(sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x3 = factor(sample(c("Control", "Treat"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x4 = factor(sample(c("Low", "High"), n, replace = TRUE), levels=c("Low", "High")),
                 x5 = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                 x6 = factor(sample(c("Group1", "Group2"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x7 = rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2),
                 x8 = rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2)) |>
        mutate(y = 5 +                          # Intercept
                   # Quantiative x1
                   2 * x1 +
                   # Categorical x2
                   (x2 == "B") * 10 +
                   # Categorical x Categorical (x3*x4)
                   (x3 == "Treat") * 5 + (x4 == "High") * 2 + 
                   (x3 == "Treat" & x4 == "High") * 15 +
                   # Quantitative x Categorical  (x5*x6)
                   3 * x5 + (x6 == "Group2") * 4 + 
                   (x5 * (x6 == "Group2")) * 8 + 
                   # Quantitative x Quantitative (x7*x8)
                   1.5 * x7 + 0.5 * x8 + 
                   0.8 * (x7 * x8) + 
                   # Error
                   rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 15))
```
:::


 \normalsize

## Part a

Fit the regression model.

\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \beta_3 I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) + \beta_4 I(x_{4i}=\text{High}) +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
       & \beta_9 (I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) ~\times~ I(x_{4i}=\text{High})) + \tag{Categorical $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\tag{Continuous $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) +
         \epsilon_i \tag{Continuous $\times$ Continuous}
\end{align*}

**Solution:** First, we fit the regression model using `lm()`.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod.q1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3*x4 + x5*x6 + x7*x8, data=dat.q1)
```
:::


 \normalsize

## Part b
Conduct a residual and outlier analysis.

 \normalsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plotResiduals(mod.q1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residual analysis for the model in Question 1.](HW3_files/figure-pdf/fig-q1b-resid-1.pdf){#fig-q1b-resid fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


 \normalsize
In @fig-q1b-resid, the residuals fall close to the line in the QQ plot and the histogram is approximately Gaussian. The fitted vs. residual plot shows an even band around zero with no pattern. Thus, the residuals appear Gaussian with mean zero and common variance.


 \normalsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plotInfluence(mod.q1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Outlier and influence analysis for the model in Question 1.](HW3_files/figure-pdf/fig-q1b-influence-1.pdf){#fig-q1b-influence fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


 \normalsize
In @fig-q1b-influence, a few observations have high leverage and a few have large studentized residuals. However, no observation has both, and all Cook's distances are far below the cutoffs. Thus, no observation has undue influence on the fit, and we do not remove any data.

## Part c
Interpret the intercept, the coefficients on $x_1$ and $x_2$.

- **Intercept** ($\widehat{\beta}_0 = 8.90$): The expected value of $Y$ when $x_1=x_5=x_7=x_8=0$ and the categorical predictors are at their baseline levels ($x_2=\text{A}$, $x_3=\text{Control}$, $x_4=\text{Low}$, $x_6=\text{Group1}$). This is not meaningful, since $x_1$, $x_7$, and $x_8$ are never near zero in the data; large standard error (26.94).

- **$x_1$** ($\widehat{\beta}_1 = 2.14$): Holding all other predictors constant, a one-unit increase in $x_1$ is associated with a 2.14 increase in the expected value of $Y$.

- **$x_2$** ($\widehat{\beta}_2 = 10.03$): Holding all other predictors constant, the expected value of $Y$ is 10.03 higher when $x_2=\text{B}$ than when $x_2=\text{A}$.

## Part d
Untangle and interpret the $x_3*x_4$ interaction using algebra. Use @tbl-q1d-emmeans and @fig-q1d-emmeans for context.


 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(emmeans)
emm.q1d <- emmeans(mod.q1, ~x3*x4) |> # Don't average across levels: use |x2*x6
            data.frame() |>
            rename("Mean"  = "emmean",
                   "Lower" = "lower.CL",
                   "Upper" = "upper.CL")
```
:::


 \normalsize


 \normalsize


::: {#tbl-q1d-emmeans .cell tbl-cap='Estimated marginal means for the model in Question 1.' tbl-align='center'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|x3      |x4   |     Mean|     SE|  df|    Lower|    Upper|
|:-------|:----|--------:|------:|---:|--------:|--------:|
|Control |Low  | 212.9676| 1.7871| 238| 209.4470| 216.4882|
|Treat   |Low  | 219.4792| 1.9123| 238| 215.7120| 223.2464|
|Control |High | 216.4894| 1.7916| 238| 212.9601| 220.0188|
|Treat   |High | 238.1930| 1.7631| 238| 234.7198| 241.6662|


:::
:::


 \normalsize


 \scriptsize


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
emm.q1d <- emm.q1d |>
  mutate(Observation = paste("(x3=", x3, ", ", "x4=", x4, ")", sep=""))
ggplot(emm.q1d) + 
  geom_point(aes(x=Mean, y=Observation))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(y=Observation,
                    xmin=Lower, xmax=Upper),
                width = 0.25)+
  # facet_wrap(~x2*x6)+
  theme_bw()+
  xlab("Estimated Mean of Y")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Estimated marginal means for the model in Question 1.](HW3_files/figure-pdf/fig-q1d-emmeans-1.pdf){#fig-q1d-emmeans fig-align='center' fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


 \normalsize

Holding the other predictors fixed, let $C$ denote the contribution of all other terms. Then

\begin{align*}
E(Y \mid \text{Control, Low}) &= C\\
E(Y \mid \text{Treat, Low}) &= C + \beta_3\\
E(Y \mid \text{Control, High}) &= C + \beta_4\\
E(Y \mid \text{Treat, High}) &= C + \beta_3 + \beta_4 + \beta_9
\end{align*}

So the effect of Treat (vs. Control) is $\beta_3$ when $x_4=\text{Low}$ and $\beta_3+\beta_9$ when $x_4=\text{High}$. That is, $\beta_9$ is the difference in the treatment effect between the High and Low groups.

- $\widehat{\beta}_3 = 6.51$: When $x_4=\text{Low}$, Treat is associated with a 6.51 higher expected $Y$ than Control.
- $\widehat{\beta}_4 = 3.52$: When $x_3=\text{Control}$, High is associated with a 3.52 higher expected $Y$ than Low.
- $\widehat{\beta}_9 = 15.19$: The treatment effect is 15.19 larger when $x_4=\text{High}$ ($6.51+15.19=21.70$) than when $x_4=\text{Low}$ ($6.51$).

These match @tbl-q1d-emmeans: $219.48-212.97=6.51$, $216.49-212.97=3.52$, and $238.19-216.49=21.70$. In @fig-q1d-emmeans, the (Treat, High) group sits well above the other three, with a confidence interval that does not overlap theirs, while the other three groups are similar. This reflects the interaction: the treatment effect is much larger when $x_4=\text{High}$.


## Part e
Untangle and interpret the $x_5*x_6$ interaction using algebra. Use @tbl-q1e-emtrends and @fig-q1e-emtrends for context.


 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
emm.q1e <- emtrends(mod.q1, var="x5", ~x5|x6) |> 
            data.frame() |>
            rename("Slope"  = "x5.trend",
                   "Lower" = "lower.CL",
                   "Upper" = "upper.CL") |>
            dplyr::select(x6, Slope, SE, df, Lower, Upper)
```
:::


 \normalsize

 \normalsize


::: {#tbl-q1e-emtrends .cell tbl-cap='Estimated marginal trends for the model in Question 1.' tbl-align='center'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|x6     |  Slope|     SE|  df|   Lower|   Upper|
|:------|------:|------:|---:|-------:|-------:|
|Group1 | 2.4835| 1.2942| 238| -0.0660|  5.0330|
|Group2 | 9.4309| 1.3367| 238|  6.7977| 12.0642|


:::
:::


 \normalsize
In @fig-q1e-emtrends, the slopes are the same and just the intercepts vary depending on $x_2$, $x_3$, and $x_4$.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
emm.q1e <- emmeans(mod.q1, ~x5*x6,
                    at = list(x5 = seq(-3, 3, length.out=500))) |> # Don't average across levels: use |x2*x3*x4
  data.frame() |>
            rename("Mean"  = "emmean",
                   "Lower" = "lower.CL",
                   "Upper" = "upper.CL")

ggplot(emm.q1e) + 
  geom_line(aes(x=x5, y=Mean, color=x6))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(x=x5, ymin=Lower, ymax=Upper, fill=x6), alpha=0.25)+
  # facet_wrap(~x2*x3*x4)+
  theme_bw()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Estimated marginal trends for the model in Question 1.](HW3_files/figure-pdf/fig-q1e-emtrends-1.pdf){#fig-q1e-emtrends fig-align='center' fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


 \normalsize

Holding the other predictors fixed, let $C$ denote the contribution of all other terms. Then

\begin{align*}
E(Y \mid x_5, \text{Group1}) &= C + \beta_5 x_5\\
E(Y \mid x_5, \text{Group2}) &= (C + \beta_6) + (\beta_5 + \beta_{10}) x_5
\end{align*}

So the slope of $x_5$ is $\beta_5$ in Group1 and $\beta_5+\beta_{10}$ in Group2. That is, $\beta_{10}$ is the difference in the slope of $x_5$ between the two groups.

- $\widehat{\beta}_5 = 2.48$: In Group1, a one-unit increase in $x_5$ is associated with a 2.48 increase in expected $Y$.
- $\widehat{\beta}_6 = 4.98$: When $x_5=0$ (its mean), Group2 has a 4.98 higher expected $Y$ than Group1.
- $\widehat{\beta}_{10} = 6.95$: The slope of $x_5$ is 6.95 larger in Group2 ($2.48+6.95=9.43$) than in Group1 ($2.48$).

These match @tbl-q1e-emtrends. Note the 95% confidence interval for the Group1 slope, $(-0.07, 5.03)$, includes zero, while the interval for the Group2 slope, $(6.80, 12.06)$, does not. In @fig-q1e-emtrends, the Group2 line is much steeper, and the lines cross near $x_5 = -4.98/6.95 \approx -0.72$. So the difference between groups depends on $x_5$.

\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial x_7} &= \beta_7 + \beta_{11} x_8\\
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial x_8} &= \beta_8 + \beta_{11} x_7
\end{align*}

So the slope of $x_7$ depends on $x_8$, and vice versa. The estimated slopes are $0.37 + 0.93x_8$ for $x_7$ and $-0.93 + 0.93x_7$ for $x_8$.

- $\widehat{\beta}_7 = 0.37$ and $\widehat{\beta}_8 = -0.93$ are the slopes when the other variable equals zero. These are not meaningful, since $x_7$ and $x_8$ are never near zero in the data.
- $\widehat{\beta}_{11} = 0.93$: For each one-unit increase in $x_8$, the slope of $x_7$ increases by 0.93 (and vice versa).

@tbl-q1f-emtrends-x7 shows the slope of $x_7$ increases from 7.92 to 9.71 to 11.50 as $x_8$ goes from one SD below its mean, to its mean, to one SD above. Similarly, @tbl-q1f-emtrends-x8 shows the slope of $x_8$ increases from 6.86 to 8.56 to 10.27. All of these confidence intervals exclude zero.

## Part g
Standardize the continuous data and refit the regression model. Redo part f. What do you notice about the coefficient estimates and why does this make the untangling process easier? 

**Solution:** First, we fit the regression model using `lm()`.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

dat.z <- dat.q1 |>
  mutate(across(c(x1, x5, x7, x8), ~ as.vector(scale(.))))
# Refit Model
mod.q1z <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3*x4 + x5*x6 + x7*x8, data=dat.z)
```

 \normalsize

After standardizing, the slopes are

\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial z_7} &= \beta_7 + \beta_{11} z_8\\
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial z_8} &= \beta_8 + \beta_{11} z_7
\end{align*}

where a one-unit change is now a one-SD change. Since $z_8=0$ corresponds to the mean of $x_8$, $\widehat{\beta}_7 = 17.86$ is the slope of $x_7$ (per SD) when $x_8$ is at its mean, and $\widehat{\beta}_8 = 16.51$ is the slope of $x_8$ (per SD) when $x_7$ is at its mean. The interaction $\widehat{\beta}_{11} = 3.29$ is how much each slope changes for a one-SD increase in the other variable (e.g., $17.86 \pm 3.29$ gives 14.57 and 21.15 in @tbl-q1-emtrends-z7).

Compared to part f, the main effects for $x_7$ and $x_8$ are now large, precisely estimated, and statistically discernible. This is because the original $\widehat{\beta}_7$ and $\widehat{\beta}_8$ described slopes at $x_8=0$ and $x_7=0$, which are far outside the data. Standardizing does not change the model fit; it moves the reference point to the mean, so the coefficients can be interpreted directly without plugging in values of the other variable.

# Question 2
@Cui25 investigate how freezing and cryogenic temperatures affect the strength, flexibility, stiffness, and internal breaking behavior of 3D-printed CF/PEEK composites.

Carbon fiber reinforced PEEK (CF/PEEK) is a high-performance composite used in 3D printing for aerospace, deep-sea, polar research. The researchers aimed to assess whether and how extremely cold environments impact this composite to understand how 3D-printed CF/PEEK performs in freezing conditions. This work would be important to understand its limits and develop preventative methods to protect against structural failures.

The researchers created fifteen 3D printed dog-bone-shaped test specimens and placed them in a chamber cooled with liquid nitrogen to $25^\circ\text{C}$, $-25^\circ\text{C}$, $-75^\circ\text{C}$, $-125^\circ\text{C}$, and $-175^\circ\text{C}$. To test strength of the specimen, a machine pulled both ends of the specimen until it snapped. 

In the table below, the researchers record the average tensile strength for three specimens from each temperature level.

| Temperature          | Mean Tensile Strength | 
| :--                  | :--                   |
| $25^\circ\text{C}$   | 81.93 MPa             |
| $-25^\circ\text{C}$  | 76.63 MPa             |
| $-75^\circ\text{C}$  | 63.23 MPa             |
| $-125^\circ\text{C}$ | 32.13 MPa             |
| $-175^\circ\text{C}$ | 12.83 MPa             |


 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat.q2 <- tibble(temp     = c(25, -25, -75, -125, -175),
                 strength = c(81.93, 76.63, 63.23, 32.13, 12.83))
x <- dat.q2$temp
y <- dat.q2$strength
n <- length(y)
```
:::


 \normalsize


## Part a
Compute the estimates we derived using calculus in lecture 16: 
\begin{align*} 
\widehat{\beta}_0 &= \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}_1 \\ 
\widehat{\beta}_1 &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i} - \bar{x}_1)(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i}-\bar{x}_1)^2}.
\end{align*}

**Solution:**

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b1.calc <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
b0.calc <- mean(y) - b1.calc * mean(x)
c(b0.calc, b1.calc)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80.7550  0.3654
```


:::
:::


 \normalsize
Using the formulas, $\widehat{\beta}_0 = 80.755$ and $\widehat{\beta}_1 = 0.3654$.


## Part b
Compute the estimates we derived using linear algebra in lecture 16: 
$$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \left(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}.$$
**Hint:** Run `?matrix()` in `R` for a quick reminder about how to create a matrix. 

**Solution:**

 \scriptsize

## Part c
Compute the maximum likelihood estimates using `optim()` in `R` as described in lecture 16:
$$\max_{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\}).$$
**Solution:**

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
neg.llik <- function(par, x, y) {
  b0    <- par[1]
  b1    <- par[2]
  sigma <- exp(par[3])                    # optimize log(sigma) so sigma > 0
  -sum(dnorm(y, mean = b0 + b1 * x, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

mle <- optim(par = c(mean(y), 0, log(sd(y))),  # starting values
             fn = neg.llik, x = x, y = y)

c(b0 = mle$par[1], b1 = mle$par[2], sigma = exp(mle$par[3]))
```


```{.r .cell-code}
# Simulate R regressions, storing the coefficient estimates
sim.coefs <- function(error.fun, R = 1000, n = 30) {
  results <- tibble(b0 = rep(NA, R), b1 = rep(NA, R))
  for (i in 1:R) {
    x <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 10)
    e <- error.fun(n)
    y <- 2 + 1.5 * x + e
    mod <- lm(y ~ x)
    results$b0[i] <- coef(mod)[1]
    results$b1[i] <- coef(mod)[2]
  }
  results
}

# Plot the sampling distributions with the true values marked
plot.coefs <- function(results) {
  p0 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = b0)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                   fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 2, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    theme_bw() + xlab(bquote(hat(beta)[0]))
  p1 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = b1)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                   fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1.5, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    theme_bw() + xlab(bquote(hat(beta)[1]))
  p0 | p1
}
```
